after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: Four rings from personal to global: a family member who moved for work; local rents, schools and languages; national rules on entry and city planning, such as China’s hukou system; and global figures of 55% urban in 2018, projected 68% by 2050, and about 304 million international migrants in mid-2024.
caption: Link levels: a national rule becomes a local issue when it changes something on the ground.

after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: Push factors drive people away from a place of origin and pull factors attract them to a destination; people move one way and remittances flow back. Migration can be internal or international. Below, definitions of urbanisation, informal settlement and brain drain.
caption: People flow one way, money often flows back.

alt: A table of six groups with a perspective and a reason: a rural family, long-standing city residents, employers, origin-country governments, destination-country governments and international bodies, noting that some states voted against or abstained on the 2018 Global Compact. Empathy does not require agreement.
caption: Even at the global level there is no single perspective on migration.

alt: A cause chain: drought reduces harvests, farm incomes fall, young adults move to the city, population grows faster than housing, and informal settlements expand. A consequence chain: remittances rise, families pay school fees, more children stay in school, but villages may lose working-age adults.
caption: Chains, not lists, and say who gains and who loses at each step.

alt: Evidence for the fictional city of Corvanna: a street survey where 288 of 400 residents (72%) agreed newcomers make housing harder to find, which shows opinion from one district; and official data showing 21,000 new households but only 9,000 new homes in five years, a gap of 12,000 that slow building could explain. Testing needs the migrant share of new households and earlier building rates.
caption: The evidence shows housing is scarce, not that newcomers are the main cause.

alt: Two options for an informal settlement. Upgrading in place tackles unsafe water and flooding and keeps residents near jobs but can be slow and face landowner objections. Relocating gives safer homes but may be far from work and break social ties, so the problem may move. Judgement: upgrading is stronger only if land rights are secured first.
caption: A strong judgement names the condition under which it holds.

alt: A table of three actions with benefits and drawbacks: investing in rural jobs and services, language and job-skills programmes for new arrivals, and ethical recruitment rules such as the non-binding 2010 WHO Global Code of Practice on recruiting health personnel.
caption: Every migration action has a trade-off to weigh.
